# Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta (Kp 8 (PTS Kp 7))
**ID:** Kp 8 (PTS Kp 7)
**Section:** Khuddakapāṭha (kp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/kp8
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0501m.mul7.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta* ("Storing Your Savings" or "Treasure-Store Discourse") is the eighth text of the *Khuddakapāṭha* in the Khuddaka Nikāya [SuttaCentral; Humphreys 1956; Collins 1998; Anālayo 2018]. The poem contrasts material wealth—which people bury underground as security against eventualities such as royal displeasure, bandits, debts, and famines, but which remains subject to theft, decay, or loss—with the imperishable "treasure" of merit (*puñña*) [Hazra 2002; Clark 2015; SuttaCentral]. Stored up through giving, moral conduct, self-restraint, and discipline (*dānena sīlena saṃyamena damena ca*), this spiritual store accompanies beings across rebirths and yields all desirable worldly and heavenly fortunes [Nyanatusita 2013; Clark 2015]. Notably, the discourse treats *nibbāna* as the culmination of these rewards, assimilating merit with final liberation, and articulates an incipient schema of three liberative attainments: the enlightenment of a disciple (*sāvaka-bodhi*), of a silent buddha (*pacceka-bodhi*), and of a supreme buddha (*buddhabhūmi* / *samyaksambodhi*) [Collins 1998; Nakamura 1980; Nyanatusita 2013].
Scholars have observed that the *Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta* is the only text in the *Khuddakapāṭha* that lacks a direct parallel in the four main Pali Nikāyas [Clark 2015]. When cited in the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 7.7), the commentator Buddhaghosa remarkedly describes the citation as having been introduced "from another tradition" (*parasamayato āharitvā dassitaṃ*) [SuttaCentral; Clark 2015]. In later exegetical tradition, the *Khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathā* draws on its seventh verse to expound the early classification of relics (*dhātu*) [Neelis 2001].
Text-reuse analyses in DharmaNexus confirm substantial internal Pali shared material with the *Khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathā* (28 matches) and a nearly identical block of verses in the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (segments 10.1–16.4) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns several verses with Mahāyāna and Āgama texts, including the Tibetan *Jātakamālā* (D4150), *Puṇyabala-avadāna* (D0347), *Bodhisattvabhūmi* (D4037), and Chinese parallels in the *Saṃyuktāgama* (T99, T100) [DharmaNexus]. Alongside other *Khuddakapāṭha* discourses, it forms part of the standard protective (*paritta*) chanting repertory and was among the earliest Pali texts translated by nineteenth-century British civil servants and scholars [Anālayo 2018; Harris 2006].
